blocks.text: Verse 5. Like the noise of chariots they will leap upon the tops of the mountains, like the noise of a flame of fire devouring stubble, like a strong people set in array for battle] This too fits locusts exactly, which fly with a great noise, [III, 309] fall upon the fields, and grind down the crops with their teeth. Hence John says of the locusts, Apoc. IX, 9. The sound of their wings was as the sound of chariots, of many horses running to battle. Pliny, book 11, chapter 29: They fly with such a whirring of wings that they are taken for other birds. Remigius of Auxerre on Joel: They make a great sound when they are sent, so much so that their sound can be heard from the sixth milestone. Cyril: Φασὶ γὰρ οὐ δίχα κτύπου πράττεσθαι παρ᾽ αὐτῶν ἐν ἀγροῖς τὴν κατάπτωσιν· ἠχὼ δέ τινα τῶν ὀδόντων ἀποτελεῖσθαι βληχρὰν, περιθραυομένων αὐταῖς τῶν πεπτωκότων, ὡς ἀνέμου φλόγα διαῤῥιπίζοντος· [Phasi gar ou dicha ktypou prattesthai par᾽ autōn en agrois tēn kataptōsin; ēchō de tina tōn odontōn apoteleisthai blēchran, perithrauomenōn autais tōn peptōkotōn, hōs anemou phloga diarrhipizontos] They say that they do not fall upon the fields without noise; and that they also produce a faint sound with their teeth while they crush the fallen crops by chewing, like that of a wind fanning a flame ^{(3)}. Moreover, a voice of their own is attributed to locusts. Thus in the Mirabilia the locust σκορπιομάχος [skorpiomachos] [col. 476], which fights the scorpion, κύκλῳ περιοῦσα τρύζει περὶ αὐτὸν [kyklō periousa tryzei peri auton], circling around it, chirps. And Aelian, book 6 of the History, ch. 19, describes βομβοῦσαν ἀκρίδα [bombousan akrida], καὶ πάρνοπα ὑποκράζοντα [kai parnopa hypokrazonta] (so I read instead of ὑποκρίζοντα [hypokrizonta] or ὑποκορίζοντα [hypokorizonta]), that is, the buzzing locust, and the parnops crying out softly. It must be admitted, however, that this voice is of uncertain origin. Pliny, in the place cited above: Their voice seems to come from the back of the head: in that place, at the joint of the shoulder blades, they are thought to have something like teeth, and by rubbing these together to produce a kind of whirring around the two equinoxes, as cicadas do around the solstice. But the same author says otherwise in ch. 51: It is indeed believed that locusts (make their sound) by the rubbing of their wings and thighs. So too the Philosopher, book 4 of the History, ch. 9: Τοῖς πηδαλίοις τρίβουσαι ποιοῦσι τὸν ψόφον [Tois pēdaliois tribousai poiousi ton psophon], They produce their noise by rubbing their hind legs. The poets attribute this voice, such as it is, to the wings. Mnesalchus, book 3 of the Anthology, ch. 24:
Οὐκ ἔτι δὴ πτερύγεσσι λιγυφθόγγοισιν ἀείσεις, Ἀκρὶ, κατ᾽ εὐκάρπους αὔλακας ἑζόμενα. [Ouk eti dē pterygessi ligyphthongoisin aeiseis, Akri, kat᾽ eukarpous aulakas hezomena.]
No longer will you sing with your sweet-sounding wings, O locust, sitting by the fruitful furrows. And again,
Ξουθᾶν ἐκ πτερύγων ἡδὺ κρέκουσα μέλος. [Xouthan ek pterygōn hēdy krekousa melos.]
Singing a sweet melody from your tawny wings. And in the same place Meleager:
Αὐτοφυὲς μίμημα λύρας, κρέκε μοί τι ποθεινὸν, Ἐκκρέουσα φίλας ποσσὶ λάλους πτέρυγας. [Autophyes mimēma lyras, kreke moi ti potheinon, Ekkreousa philas possi lalous pterygas.]
[III, 310] O you who by nature imitate the lyre, sing me something lovely, striking with your feet your dear vocal wings. And Phaennus:
Δαμοκρίτῳ μὲν ἐπὼ λιγυρὰν ὄκα Μοῦσαν ἐνίην Ἀκρὶς ἀπὸ πτερύγων, τὸν βαθὺν ὕπνον ἄγων. [Damokritō men epō ligyran oka Mousan eniēn Akris apo pterygōn, ton bathyn hypnon agōn.]

For Damocritus, when I, the locust, sent forth a sweet Muse from my wings, bringing on deep sleep. Nor should you be surprised that a voice in which there seems to be no elegance at all is praised. For the poets everywhere praise the locust, like the cicada, for its song. Leonidas:
Ἀκρίδι, τᾷ κατ᾽ ἄρουραν ἀηδόνι, καὶ δρυοκοίτᾳ Τέττιγι ξυνὸν τύμβον ἔτευξε Μυρώ. [Akridi, ta kat᾽ arouran aēdoni, kai dryokoita Tettigi xynon tymbon eteuxe Myrō.]
For the locust, the nightingale of the fields, and for the cicada that lies in the oaks, Myro made a common tomb. Anyte:
Οὐκ ἔτι λιγεία σε κατ᾽ ἀφνεὸν Ἄκιδος οἶκον, Ἀκρὶ, μελιζομέναν, ὄψεται ἠέλιος. [Ouk eti ligeia se kat᾽ aphneon Akidos oikon, Akri, melizomenan, opsetai ēelios.]

No longer, O tuneful locust, will the sun see you singing by the rich house of Acis. And much earlier Theocritus, Idyll 7, belittling himself (ἐξουθενίζων [exouthenizōn]) as unequal to a contest with a poet of great name:
— βάτραχος δὲ ποτ᾽ ἀκρίδας, ὥς τις ἐρίσδω· [— batrachos de pot᾽ akridas, hōs tis erisdō;]

Like a frog against locusts I compete. Nor was there any need to understand cicadas, whom he praises elsewhere for their song. For among locusts too there are some αἱ συρίζουσιν ἐναρμόνιον [hai syrizousin enarmonion], which produce a harmonious whistling, as the Scholiast says there. Accordingly in Idyll 5 Lacon invites Comatas to rest in the nearby wood for this reason:
Ψυχρὸν ὕδωρ τηνεὶ καταλείβεται· ὧδε πεφύκει Ποία, χᾀ στιβὰς ᾇδε, καὶ ἀκρίδες ὧδε λαλεῦντι. [Psychron hydōr tēnei kataleibetai; hōde pephykei Poia, cha stibas hade, kai akrides hōde laleunti.]
Cold water flows there; there grass has grown, and a couch, and locusts there chatter, or sing.
